title: Annualisation
body:
**Annualisation** converts a statistic computed on daily data into the yearly figure that
finance reports by convention, so that numbers from different sampling frequencies are
comparable.

The factor is $\sqrt{252}$ for a standard deviation, where 252 is the approximate number of
trading days in a year:

```
√252 = 15.875

daily volatility 1.2%   ->   annualised 19.05%
```

The square root is the part worth understanding. Variances add across independent periods and
standard deviations do not, so a variance over $n$ days is $n$ times the daily variance and the
standard deviation is $\sqrt{n}$ times the daily one.

That is the same relationship as the standard error $\sigma/\sqrt{n}$ in the
[[Central Limit Theorem]] from [[STATISTICS]], used in the opposite direction: there
it shrinks an estimate's uncertainty as data accumulates, and here it grows a spread as the
horizon lengthens.

Returns scale with $n$ where a standard deviation scales with $\sqrt{n}$, so the
[[Sharpe Ratio]], being one divided by the other, scales by $n/\sqrt{n} = \sqrt{n}$ as
well.

The assumption underneath is that returns on different days are independent, which is
approximately true and fails during a crisis, when consecutive days become correlated and
annualising understates the real risk.
